name: Eyelash growth serum (peptide, OTC)

lead: Peptide lash serums are over-the-counter products applied to the lash line, aimed at longer, thicker, fuller lashes that frame the eyes. They are often positioned as non-prescription alternatives to prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), a prostaglandin analogue.

Lashes differ from scalp hair: their length is largely genetically set, follicle number cannot increase after birth, and length, thickness and darkness decline with age. Some brands use peptides instead of prostaglandins because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California. No published human trials of the peptide products were found; trial data exist for bimatoprost.

paras: The serum is brushed along the base of the lashes, usually daily over weeks. Forum users ask for brand recommendations, report mixed results, and compare it with castor oil, rosemary oil, minoxidil and Latisse.
Safety data on specific peptide serums are limited. Eye-area products carry general irritation risks, and prescription bimatoprost has documented effects such as redness and eyelid darkening.

angle.text: Users apply these drug-free serums along the lash line hoping for longer, thicker lashes that frame the eyes and make them look fuller and more defined. They are sold as alternatives to prescription prostaglandin products. Trials exist for prescription bimatoprost, not for the peptide versions.

lead: Over-the-counter eyelash growth serums are cosmetic liquids or gels brushed along the lash line to help lashes look longer, thicker, darker and fuller. They are sold as drug-free alternatives to prescription prostaglandin products and typically list peptides, conditioning agents, botanical extracts or vitamins as their key ingredients instead of a prostaglandin analogue.[1][2]

People use them as one step in a lash routine that can also include mascara, curlers, tints, extensions or prescription bimatoprost. Fuller, darker, longer lashes frame the eyes and are widely discussed as part of eye-area attractiveness; Wikipedia notes that lash length has been studied both for its protective function and for its effect on perceived attractiveness.[1] Because lash length is largely genetically set and declines with age, a product that changes how lashes look appeals to people who want a change without a prescription.[1]

Published research on peptide lash serums is small. One open-label, single-center study of a peptide-containing serum in 29 women reported gains in lash length, thickness and curl over 90 days.[3] The large placebo-controlled trial data in this area concern prescription bimatoprost (Latisse), a different product class.[4] On looksmax.org the serums are discussed alongside Latisse, castor oil, rosemary oil and minoxidil.

paras: Peptide lash serums are sold by many cosmetic brands, from mass-market skincare lines to specialist lash companies. Manufacturers describe the products as supporting lash health or the appearance of lash length and density. Some are water-based, which forum users say feels different from oil-based remedies when applied. They are applied with a thin brush or applicator, usually along the base of the upper lashes, typically once nightly, and are used over weeks.

Over the past decade, according to Wikipedia, lash conditioners and growth products have multiplied, often built around seed extracts, minerals and other compounds, with some companies drawing on research into prostaglandins and Wnt/beta-catenin signalling.[1] Peptides are short chains of amino acids; in lash products, brands describe them as keratin-supporting or follicle-supporting ingredients. One commonly named ingredient is myristoyl pentapeptide-17, which suppliers promote for lash and brow products.[3]

Eyelashes grow from follicles on the lid margin in up to six layers. The number of follicles is fixed during embryonic development and cannot be increased after birth, and individual lashes grow back in roughly seven to eight weeks if pulled out.[1]

Upper lashes typically measure 7 to 8 mm, with a range of about 3 to 10 mm between individuals, and length is almost entirely determined by genetics. Lash length, thickness and darkness decrease with age. Lash hair is not androgen-dependent and is therefore not affected by puberty.[1] These features frame what any lash product can influence: the condition of existing lashes and, for prescription drugs, the growth phase.

Latisse (bimatoprost ophthalmic solution 0.03%, Allergan) was approved by the FDA in late December 2008 as the first treatment for eyelash hypotrichosis, meaning inadequate or sparse lashes.[4] Bimatoprost had been approved in the US in 2001 for glaucoma and ocular hypertension; the cosmetic indication followed, with the product applied to the skin at the base of the upper lashes rather than dropped into the eye.[2] Reported adverse effects of bimatoprost include eye redness, eyelid and periorbital skin darkening and, with eye-drop use, permanent iris darkening.[2]

Peptide serums are a separate product category, and the Latisse figures do not describe them. Wikipedia reports that some cosmetic brands use peptides instead of prostaglandins, reportedly because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California; the statement in that article is itself sourced to a retailer blog.[1]

Dermatology Times reported that the phase 3 trial enrolled 278 adults with minimal or moderate lash prominence, who applied Latisse or placebo nightly to the upper lid margins for 16 weeks; it reported a mean improvement of more than 100% over baseline in lash thickness, and no significant intraocular pressure lowering in the trial.[4] Dermatologists quoted in the same article raised questions about redness, lid-margin irritation, skin discoloration and the fact that a four-month trial cannot show iris pigmentation changes that may take longer to appear.[4]

In the US, a product whose labelling says it will increase lash growth can be treated as a drug rather than a cosmetic. In November 2007 the FDA, through the US Marshals Service, seized 12,682 applicator tubes of Age Intervention Eyelash, sold by Jan Marini Skin Research, which contained bimatoprost. The agency described it as an unapproved, misbranded drug and an adulterated cosmetic and said the extra bimatoprost could reduce the effectiveness of glaucoma medication, with possible effects on the optic nerve, macula and uvea. The company said it had stopped making bimatoprost versions the year before.[5] Peptide serums on the market are sold as cosmetics and do not list prostaglandin analogues as actives.

sections.h: Other ways people change lash appearance
paras: Wikipedia lists several non-serum options: mascara and eyeliner, curlers and perms that make lashes look longer from the front without lengthening them, tints, eyelash extensions and false lashes (popular since the 1960s), and lash transplants using scalp hair, which keep growing like scalp hair and need trimming.[1] Kohl to darken the lid edge dates to the Bronze Age, and long lashes were prized in ancient Rome.[1] Serums sit alongside these as a product aimed at the lashes themselves.

A 90-day open-label, single-center study published in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology in 2020 enrolled 30 healthy Indian women aged 15 to 45, 29 of whom finished. Participants applied a multi-ingredient 'polygrowth factor' serum nightly to the lid margins, and assessments at days 30, 60 and 90 included ophthalmological and dermatological exams and digital imaging. Compared with baseline, the authors reported improvements in length (10.52%), volume (9.3%), luster (11.43%), thickness (35%) and curl (50.83%), with no product-related adverse events. The authors called for larger randomized controlled studies; the study had no control group, and the serum is listed by the publication host, a peptide supplier, as containing myristoyl pentapeptide-17.[3]

Manufacturers of individual serums also cite their own consumer or ingredient-supplier studies; these generally are not published in peer-reviewed journals. Controlled lash-growth trials in the literature concern prostaglandin analogues such as bimatoprost, a different class of product.[2][4]

Eye-area products can cause irritation or allergic reactions, as with any cosmetic applied near the eye. For the prescription counterpart, Wikipedia notes infection risk if single-use applicators are reused and darkening of the lid or skin beneath the eye.[2] The 2007 FDA action concerned bimatoprost added to a product sold as a cosmetic, not a peptide serum.[5] Product labels typically advise stopping use if irritation occurs.

Threads on looksmax.org ask which lash serum to use and whether results are visible. One user who had used castor oil for a month reported that lashes looked healthier but not thicker and asked about serums; a reply suggested Latisse. Another thread asks whether a water-based serum from a mass-market skincare brand works, with the poster comparing it to rosemary oil they said felt more saturating. Other threads compare lash serums with oral minoxidil, and one reply says topical minoxidil is not recommended for lashes.
Lashes are usually discussed as a small but visible part of eye-area aesthetics; users treat serums as a low-effort addition to routines that include other grooming steps.

lore.intro: In forum discussion, lash serums are treated as a milder or more accessible option than prescription bimatoprost, with mixed reports of results.
